title: Taking the lease on a session, using it, and giving it back

expect.why: A lease cannot be taken on a session in open mode, so every hijack scenario has to move it first. The mode is reported back, which is how a caller knows the change took.
The lease is granted. This is the single most load-bearing operation in the product: it decides who may type into somebody else's terminal.
A boolean, not a string and not the number one — the field a client branches on before it starts sending keystrokes.
The answer names the worker whose lease was taken, so a client holding several cannot mix them up.
The owner is echoed back as given. A port that substituted its own default would make the audit trail wrong about who took control.
A lease has an expiry, and it is a number rather than a formatted time — clients compare it against their own clock. Its value is volatile; that it is a number is not.
Extending a lease is what stops a long operation being interrupted by its own timeout.
The heartbeat is acknowledged, so a client can tell an extension that worked from one that silently did not.
The holder of the lease can read the screen. This is what an operator or an agent acts on, so a port that could take a lease but not read through it would be useless.
The client library's own reading. The screen itself is volatile — it is a live terminal — but that the read succeeded is not.
Giving the lease back is what lets anyone else have it. A release that silently failed would strand the session until the lease expired.
Acknowledged, rather than accepted in silence.
A lease released twice is gone, not forbidden: the second call refers to something that no longer exists. 409 would suggest it is still held by somebody.

The lease routes answer with an `error` key where the session routes answer with `detail`. Both envelopes are the reference's and a client has to know both — which is exactly what the Go client got wrong, reading only `error` and rendering the whole body as its message.
